findings.title: The raw ES `_id` is used as the saved-object id, so `_source` decryption always fails.
findings.body: The ES `_id` of a saved-object document is the raw id from the serializer (`<type>:<id>`, or `<namespace>:<type>:<id>` for single-namespace types), not the saved object's id. Encrypted attributes are bound to `{id, type, namespace}` through AAD. Passing the raw id therefore makes every decryption fail with an AAD mismatch, logs an error per row, and strips the attributes. Single-namespace types also store `namespace`, not `namespaces`, so the namespace part of the AAD is wrong as well. Turn the raw id back into the saved-object id and namespace with the serializer (`rawToSavedObject` or `isRawSavedObject`/`generateRawId` logic) before calling `decryptOrStripResponseAttributes`.

findings.title: Docs promise encrypted columns are always nulled, but stripping only matches column names.
findings.body: The tests show that stripping is decided by the output column name (`<type>.<encryptedAttr>`). A pipeline such as `| EVAL s = connector.secrets | KEEP s`, `| RENAME connector.secrets AS s`, or `CONCAT`/`STATS VALUES(...)` on the attribute returns a column with a different name. That column passes through with the raw ciphertext. So the claim "Always replaced with `null`" is false, and consumers who rely on it will leak encrypted values. Either make the post-processing reject or null any column derived from encrypted fields (for example, by refusing pipelines that reference encrypted attribute paths), or change the docs to say this is not guaranteed. I could not see `esql.ts`, which may have a check I don't know about.

findings.title: Without an `_id` column, `_source` comes back with the encrypted attributes untouched.
findings.body: This test makes it expected behaviour that a response with a `_source` column but no `_id` column (for example, `metadata: ['_source']` or `| DROP _id`) skips decryption entirely. It only asserts that decryption was not called and never asserts that `index-pattern.secret` was stripped. When `_source` can't be decrypted, the encrypted attributes should be removed from it, matching the docs' 'stripped on failure' rule. As written, the raw ciphertext reaches the caller. Strip encrypted attributes from `_source` whenever decryption is not possible, and assert that `secret` is undefined in this test.

findings.title: The pipeline check doesn't stop callers from changing which indices are queried.
findings.body: The only check is a regex that rejects a pipeline starting with `FROM`/`ROW`/`SHOW`/`METRICS`. The pipeline is then pasted straight after the generated `FROM` clause (line 114), so it can still change the source. A pipeline like `, other-index | ...` or `METADATA _index | ...` appends more indices or metadata to the `FROM`. A pipeline like `| LOOKUP JOIN some_lookup_index ON ...` or `| ENRICH policy` pulls data from indices the namespace `filter` never applies to. The query runs as the repository's internal client, not as the end user. Require the pipeline to start with `|` once leading whitespace is trimmed. Parse it with the ES|QL parser and reject source-changing commands (`LOOKUP JOIN`, `ENRICH`, subqueries), or allow only an explicit list of processing commands. I could not check which lookup indices or enrich policies the kibana system user can read.

findings.title: Elasticsearch errors are passed through raw instead of being turned into saved-object errors.
findings.body: `rawClient.esql.query` is called with no error handling. An invalid pipeline (ES returns 400), a missing index (404) or an unsupported-server error reaches the caller as a raw `ResponseError`. Other repository APIs convert these with `SavedObjectsErrorHelpers` (`decorateEsError`) and check for a supported ES server. HTTP routes therefore return a 500 for a bad pipeline instead of a 400. Calling the raw client also skips the retry and error handling that `RepositoryEsClient` adds. Wrap the call in try/catch and convert the error with `decorateEsError`, as `search`/`find` do.

findings.title: Encrypted values are only nulled when the output column has the exact original name.
findings.body: `stripEncryptedColumns` nulls a column only when its name is exactly `<type>.<encryptedAttr>`. A pipeline such as `| EVAL x = \`type.secret\``, `| RENAME \`type.secret\` AS x`, `| STATS v = VALUES(\`type.secret\`)` or `| EVAL x = CONCAT(...)` returns the stored encrypted value under a different name, and it is not removed. The same gap exists for `_source`. When `_source` is requested without `_id` (line 148), or copied or renamed with EVAL, it is returned with the raw ciphertext still in it, whereas `find` strips those attributes. This matters when an encrypted attribute is mapped, or when ES|QL reads unmapped fields from `_source`. Reject pipelines that reference encrypted attribute fields, or block `_source` and encrypted fields up front, instead of filtering output columns by name.

findings.title: The example comment says a `WHERE` clause is generated, but security filtering goes through `filter`.
findings.body: The comment says `generates: FROM .kibana METADATA _id, _source | WHERE ...`. The same doc and the unit tests (`/^FROM .+ METADATA _id, _source \| LIMIT 10$/`) show that no `WHERE` is added: the namespace and type restrictions go into the request's `filter` parameter instead. Change the comment to show the actual generated query.
